toc.title: Step one: validate, normalize, and give permission
Step two: find safety while you're in shutdown
Step three: strengthen your vagal brake
Step four: prepare for the return of sympathetic energy

blocks.p: You're experiencing symptoms of depression: a lack of motivation, an inability to experience happiness, reduced life satisfaction, isolating yourself, oversleeping, losing hope, and more. In your quest to find out what the heck is going on, you learned about the Polyvagal Theory and this thing called dorsal vagal shutdown, and things are starting to make sense. So the next question is: how do I heal? How do I come out of shutdown?

There are a lot of people in shutdown who really want and are ready to learn more, so I'm going to cover what shutdown is only briefly, and focus primarily on the recovery side: the overall process of coming out of shutdown, and then four major steps.

Dorsal vagal shutdown is a state of the autonomic nervous system, along with safety and along with flight and fight. Basically, the body can be in a state of safety and connection, it can be mobile, or it can be immobile. Shutdown is immobility.

In this state, the body is preparing for death. It's conserving resources. And it actually increases the chances of survival by mimicking a corpse. If a predator comes along and sees what looks to be a corpse, it's probably more likely to mosey on by and ignore it, or to use its own fight energy to keep chasing down whatever it's already chasing.

Shutdown happens when safety has not worked. Dealing with a dangerous situation through social engagement hasn't worked. Running away has not worked or is not likely. Fight has not worked or is not likely. So the last resort is shutdown. Freeze and shutdown are different. Shutdown is part of freeze, but here we're focusing on shutdown itself, the last resort.
The way to understand these states is that the safety state is all about connection. Flight and fight are about mobility. And shutdown is about immobility and disconnection.

Here's the top-down understanding, something to frame everything else in. To come out of a dorsal vagal shutdown, you mindfully allow the shutdown, and then climb your [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system).

Because shutdown is about disconnection, coming out of shutdown requires reconnecting. Reconnecting is the goal: reconnecting with yourself, reconnecting with your environment, and maybe even reconnecting with others in your life who are safe.

The other piece I think is really important is that we don't want to fight it. Yes, it's difficult. It sucks. There's pain there. There's a reason you're in shutdown. You probably feel very alone. Probably very sad and depressed, isolated, maybe rejected, maybe abandoned. Being alone sucks. I know it's hard. But regardless of all that, we don't want to fight it. To eventually come out of it, you do need to mindfully experience it. Right now that probably sounds like way too much, and you're probably right. But there are ways to actually feel it, even though it's difficult, and come out of it.

One thing that can help is focusing on safety. Say you did nothing else. You didn't feel your shutdown at all, you just focused on being more and more in your safety state. That can help. The shutdown flavor might still linger, but maybe not as dominant. It's probably still going to flavor your system, but I think the negative impact of it will be a lot less. A lot of good can happen just from building your safety state.

Mindfulness is extremely important, because it allows natural self-regulation to unfold. It gives your body, your autonomic nervous system, permission to do that polyvagal ladder climbing. Our bodies are always wanting to, striving toward, self-regulation. We are biological organisms that must reach homeostasis in order to use our bodily resources optimally. Mindfulness allows that natural potential to unfold.

Mindfulness means being anchored in safety and then allowing whatever is happening inside of us to happen. That means we can't be judging and blaming ourselves. As much as possible, we want to reduce the cognitions in our heads. That's very hard to do, yes, but there are things that help, like focusing on the present moment and on the environment. We'll get to those.

So in order to self-regulate, we first have to mindfully allow the process of self-regulation to happen. That requires being in our safety state and then mindfully experiencing what it's like to be in shutdown. That opens up the natural process: climbing the ladder and accessing more and more of your safety state.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.h: Step one: validate, normalize, and give permission

blocks.p: The first step is actually three mini steps.

1A. Validate. Validate your emotions and also the cognitions of shutdown. That means simply acknowledging that they are real, without denying them. If you shared with a friend how you feel and they said, "Yeah, you do feel that way. I hear that you feel that way," you'd probably feel validated. You'd feel recognized. So admit to yourself that yes, you do feel sad, or lost, or disconnected, or alone, or rejected, or whatever emotions come with your shutdown. And the judgments and blaming I mentioned: validate that those are real too. You are doing that, and it does come from your shutdown state.

1B. Normalize. Normalizing is just recognizing that you exist in shutdown for a reason. It's not random. We don't want to get sucked into the story of your shutdown or how you got here. We don't want to go deep into that right now at all. Instead, just reflect on your life in general and ask yourself: does it make sense that I live in a shutdown state? If yes, congratulations, you have just normalized yourself. Great job.
1C. Give permission. Give your shutdown permission to exist. It's valid. It's normal. So let it be there.

If you cannot do the pieces of step one, I don't think you're ready for step two, and I would not encourage you to go on. Instead, focus on finding your safety state, feeling it, connecting with it, and practicing being in it as much as you possibly can. As you gain more safety, the validation, normalization, and giving permission might become more approachable. And like I said, it is possible to feel more safety, and get relief, without directly feeling the shutdown. A lot of good can be done for your daily functioning, your relationships, and your life satisfaction just by focusing on your safety state.

blocks.h: Step two: find safety while you're in shutdown

blocks.p: Let's say you have a strong enough safety state, or enough curiosity, and you're ready for step two. Now you find safety while you're in shutdown, so both experiences are present: the shutdown, and safety in your system too.

This tells your nervous system, your body, that it's okay to come out of shutdown. Maybe not long term yet. That's something we keep practicing and building the capacity for. But at least in this present moment, being in safety tells your body, "Hey, it's okay to come out of shutdown now."

We don't want it to be an overwhelming experience. We want to come out of shutdown a little bit at a time, so a long process is very normal, and actually kind of ideal. If coming out of shutdown is overwhelming, that might send you right back into shutdown and really reinforce it.

I think a major part of this is allowing shutdown in the right environment. Remember, coming out of shutdown is about reconnecting, and the right environment helps you connect with the environment itself.

The right environment probably involves less stimulation. Calm and quiet is generally better than loud. Dim lighting is generally better than bright lighting, especially fake, fluorescent white lighting, though natural sunlight can definitely help as well. People in shutdown tend to really gravitate toward rainy, cloudy days. They do well in those environments. A day at the beach that's mild, coolish, even overcast, is another one people seem drawn to. You may very well love a beach when it's super bright, with people around and lots of noise. If you can do that in shutdown, great, go ahead. I don't know the right answer for you. This is generally what I see the people I work with in therapy gravitate toward.

Then consider who's there. Generally, people in shutdown seem to prefer solitude. Solitude and isolation are different. Isolation means you're alone, but there's a chaotic or fearful energy to it, like you're trying to get away from people. Solitude means you're choosing to be alone, you prefer it, and it feels right. You're grounded in your safety state, you're alone, and you're okay with it.
For myself, shutdown's my home away from home. I do better when I'm alone a lot of the time. I need at least some alone time every day, it seems.

So that lower-stimulation environment, in solitude, seems to be a good fit for people in shutdown. Being alone on a beach where there's no one around generally seems better than when it's crowded. Being alone in a park generally seems better than when people are around. Although people watching can be helpful for someone in shutdown too, or hearing the laughter of kids on the playground, or birds chirping. Those can all be safety cues. Again, notice what works best for you: the right environment, and whether or not you want people around.

Co-regulation from safe others can be a really good piece of coming out of shutdown as well. This is connection again, connecting with others. Not through force. We don't want someone yelling in your face, "Hey, snap out of it!" That's overwhelming, and it's going to send you right back into shutdown. We want someone who's there by you, there with you. That might be a trusted loved one, or a professional like a therapist. Maybe it's a community, even a virtual one, or a club you're part of. It could also come through a pet you can connect with: touch, petting, eye contact. There's a sense of warmth and connection there.
Deb Dana said this on the podcast:

q: In the beginning, for many people, climbing out of dorsal is really difficult... They need a co-regulator. They need somebody to accompany them.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: The other thing that helps is using your senses in an environment that feels safer. This is a chance to connect with the environment, and also with yourself. Focusing on and connecting with the external environment can really help calm down those cognitions of blame, judgment, or pessimism. It keeps you in the here and now instead of in the judgments in your head.

So notice the safety in the environment, and then, if you can, notice how that safety affects you internally. For people in shutdown, looking inward can be quite a challenge, because there are often dissociative elements: a significant disconnection from yourself, your body, how you feel, the sensations within, even the emotions. So just notice how you feel inside as you take in the environment through your senses.

For example, if you're with your pet, I don't want you to just exist with your pet in the same room. Be with them. Experience the warmth of their body as they lie next to you, or the weight of their body across your lap, or the texture of their fur as you pet them. Immerse yourself in the sensory experience of being with your pet.
If you have a candle in the room that you like, mindfully experience it. Inhale, breathe it in, and notice how it feels. Notice the sensation of liking the smell.

Even if you're in a really deep shutdown and stuck in one place, use your eyes. Notice what's happening around you. Look at the lights and shadows in your space, the highlights as they bounce off the surfaces. As best you can, immerse yourself in the details of your environment, then ask yourself how you feel about them, and notice any safety that might be present within you. That might just be: do you like it or not? If it's that simple, that's fine. That's a step forward.

blocks.h: Step three: strengthen your vagal brake

blocks.p: Step three is a much longer-term goal and practice: working on the strength of your vagal brake. The vagal brake is the influence of your safety state on your heart. It keeps your heart at a calmer pace.

For someone in shutdown, the heartbeat is already at a pretty darn calm pace. That's not really the issue. What a strong vagal brake does is allow for ladder climbing in the longer term. When you come out of shutdown, the first thing you're going to feel is the activation of flight and fight. If you continually practice being in your safety state and develop the strength of your vagal brake, you'll be more prepared to handle that returning energy as you climb into flight and fight.
Basically: practice being in safety, identify what brings you to safety, and keep practicing it little by little.

If you skip this and just try to feel shutdown and come out of it, it likely won't result in anything really positive. The returning flight and fight energy will probably be overwhelming and send you right back into shutdown, and that's what we don't want. As that energy comes up, you might turn to some behavior to cope or self-soothe, like binge eating, or even self-harm, or something else. Thoughts might come in: "I knew I would fail. What's the point of all this?" So don't underestimate the vagal brake. Please put the time into developing and strengthening your safety state.

blocks.h: Step four: prepare for the return of sympathetic energy

blocks.p: Step four builds on the last one. As you come out of shutdown into flight and fight, you're probably going to feel fight first. That's typically what I see with my therapy clients, and it makes sense: going down the polyvagal ladder, you go from safety to flight to fight and then shutdown. Coming out of it means going into fight first, then flight, then safety.
So irritation and anger often come with coming out of shutdown. Generally it's a good sign, but it also tells us we need more safety in the system.

When you come out of shutdown into fight energy, ideally you experience it as power, not as anger. Anger is not a bad thing, but it can be dysregulated. Power is fight energy with healthy boundaries and expectations. To me, that's the difference between regulated and dysregulated fight energy.

Coming out of shutdown into power has a sense of connection to it, because you're able to hold healthy boundaries, which involves connecting with somebody and also connecting with yourself and your values. More dysregulated anger, to me, is about disconnection. You're trying to dominate, or get someone to back off, more out of fear than out of empathy or compassion. Healthy boundaries with power can have empathy and compassion, and a sense of connection with the other person, even while you're enforcing a boundary.

Besides continually working on your safety state, something that might help is noticing which movements you're pulled toward. As you come out of shutdown, your body becomes more mobile, and you'll probably have more of an impulse to move in some way. It's different for everybody. A lot of the people I work with want to go to the gym and work out. Me, I prefer to get in the pool, kick off the walls, and do this tai chi kind of stuff with my hands in the water. Some people want to do yoga. I don't know the right answer for you. Listen to what feels right inside of you. You can also notice whether there's an impulse to be with somebody, to go to the gym or do yoga together, or whether it's something you need to do in solitude. Either one is fine.

Allow those movements and impulses to emerge, but also notice the micro moments, and mindfully allow those too. As you come out of shutdown, you might have little moments of wanting to connect with people: making eye contact, smiling. You might have more mobility that lets you go for a walk. These may not be huge, obvious changes, but they're signals that you have more energy in your system and more of an impulse to connect. So look for the little ones, and look for the big ones too, where you have an impulse to do something with your returning fight and flight energy.
